title: Decide the CodeFlow delivery system before 3.0.0
summary: Six stage figures and six decisions on the CodeFlow delivery system before 3.0.0.

blocks.title: Every stage of work gets a guard
blocks.caption: Each stage of work, the failure the audit found there today, and the guard that closes it: registry, ready rule, status commands, acceptance checks, release checks, fixed notes, and adopter profiles.

blocks.markdown: CodeFlow 3.0.0 is held until project management, changelog and version management hold up when agents work in parallel. The figure is the proposal in one view: each stage of work gets a guard for the failure the audit found there. Fable, Astra and Grok 4.7 designed it independently; I merged the three designs, and all three reviewed the merge twice and now agree. Nothing is built yet. Six decisions below are yours. Use **Comment** on any figure, row or decision you disagree with.

**What "registry" means here.** It is not a GitHub feature or a separate service. It is an ordinary git branch, `codeflow/registry`, in the same repository as the code, that never merges into `main`. "Registry" is the job the branch does: it holds one tiny file per number ever issued, saying which record owns it. It is safe because GitHub protects the branch itself from deletion and history rewrites, and CodeFlow's own checks guard the files inside it (details below).

blocks.title: How a task number is issued
blocks.caption: Two agents ask for a number at once.

blocks.markdown: Numbers stay readable (`TSK-100`). The registry is a branch, `codeflow/registry`, holding one small file per number ever issued. Git accepts a push only if nobody pushed since you looked, so two agents cannot both win. Each new record also carries a hidden random `uid`, and CI refuses to merge a record whose number is not registered to its own `uid`. It is the same for every project that adopts CodeFlow: each repository that tracks work gets its own registry branch with the same protections. Numbers are scoped to their repository, as today, so `TSK-100` in an adopting project and `TSK-100` in CodeFlow are unrelated.

blocks.summary: What keeps the registry from getting messed up

items: GitHub protects the branch from deletion and history rewrites. It does not protect the files inside it: an ordinary commit can delete a number's file (Fable and Astra both reproduced this).
So the next number is one more than the highest ever issued in the branch history. Deleting a file cannot bring a number back.
CodeFlow's pre-push hook and git-guard refuse registry pushes that remove or edit a file. A CI job re-checks every registry push, and no new number is issued while damage is unrepaired.
Offline: the reservation is written locally as pending and published by the next online command. If the number was taken meanwhile, the unmerged record is renumbered before it lands.
Forks and hand-written records: a maintainer registers them with `codeflow ids admit`; the PR stays red until then.
Hosts without branch protection: damage is detected afterwards, not prevented, and `codeflow doctor` says so.
Not yet proven on a real GitHub repository. TSK-100 does that first; if it fails, the work stops and decision 1 returns to you.

blocks.summary: Has this been done before? Prior art and research

items: Research covered beads, git-bug, git-appraise, Spec Kit, Kiro, BMAD, task-master, Changesets and towncrier (research-delivery-systems.md, with sources).

Closest precedent: beads, an issue tracker for coding agents, moved its data to a dedicated sync branch and later deleted that code (about 11,000 lines) for a database. Its failures came from keeping mutable issue state apart from the code and merging it: silent data loss, resurrected state, issues closed while their PR was open.

This design differs on exactly those points: the branch holds only append-only number reservations, never status or content, and is never merged. Records and their status stay with the code, in the same PR.

The research report rated a shared registry as right for many parallel issuers with an owner for the infrastructure. The building blocks are proven; this exact combination has no precedent we found. That is why TSK-100 proves it first and option 1b is the fallback.
Branch protection covers public repositories on every GitHub plan, and private ones only on Pro, Team or Enterprise. A repository admin can switch it off, so agents run without admin rights.

blocks.title: What a task stores, and what is computed
blocks.caption: Task states.

blocks.markdown: Records store only decisions: blocked, complete or cancelled, and why. What git already knows is computed on demand: whether work has started, whether a task is ready or waiting, and how far an epic has got. The validator refuses a transition that lacks its item, whoever edits the file. `work next`, `work start`, `status` and CI use one ready rule, and `work claim` pushes a task branch so other agents can see the task is taken.

Any change to something an adopting project runs must test that real path. The checker proves structure and binding, not honesty; that stays with the reviewer and your merge.

blocks.title: Where each check runs

columns.title: Fixed once a project tracks work
columns.markdown:
- Unique numbers; the registry only grows
- Blocked needs a reason; done needs evidence
- Criteria cannot change inside the task's own PR
- Every PR names its task, or says why it needs none
- Secret scan, protected branches, no AI attribution: never exempt

columns.title: Adjustable by the project
columns.markdown:
- Acceptance and journey checks: block or warn, never off
- Own record templates
- Own PR template, mapped to CodeFlow's sections with a warning period
- Own release tool (Changesets, release-please and others), or none
- Bots confirmed by CI skip format checks

blocks.markdown: **How work flows: the five gaps and the proposed rules.** Numbers match the dots in the figure.

rows: No record. Research is a route mode that stops without product edits; findings land ad hoc in docs/verification or docs/plan. A spike is a branch prefix and a work_type, but work start only runs on task/ branches.

Findings go in docs/research/, one file per question with its sources. A spec, ADR or epic cites them in an inputs list. A spike is a task with work_type spike on a spike/ branch; it lands its findings, never its code.
An epic lists specs and a task adds its own. Nothing says whether one spec may serve several epics; spec new --for links only one. In practice every spec has one consumer.

Many to many, stated. A spec is the behaviour contract; an epic delivers part or all of it, so one spec can span a 3.0 slice and a 3.1 epic, and one epic can draw on several specs. An epic with no spec is fine for cleanup or operations work; its own criteria carry the acceptance.

The contract says a spec freezes as implemented when its consumers ship. Nothing checks it: SPC-002 is still draft though EPC-002 is complete, and SPC-009 is approved though EPC-008 is complete. Freezing is undefined when a spec has several consumers.
Criteria freeze at approval and change only by a reviewed plan change. Implemented is computed when every consumer is complete, never set by hand, so it cannot go stale.
A task without an epic needs a standalone_reason. Capabilities list epics only, so a standalone task can never reach one. Two sources give different tests for when a task may stand alone.
One test in one place: a task may stand alone when its outcome is one reviewable PR. It may list capabilities and specs directly.
Enforced today: exactly one epic or a stated reason; dependencies resolve and have no cycles; specs must be approved before work starts.
Kept as is, plus the readiness and acceptance rules already in this design.

blocks.title: 1. How should numbers stay unique?
blocks.markdown:
- **(a) The registry branch** (recommended). Readable numbers, unique the moment they are issued when the agent is online. Two tasks on the longest chain; depends on the host proof.
- **(b) Scan all branches, catch clashes in CI.** Smallest; two machines can still pick one number, and one record is renumbered before merge. This is the fallback if the proof fails.
- **(c) Random ids for everything.** No coordination; long ids, and every branch name, link and habit changes.

blocks.title: 2. Should claiming a task lock it?
blocks.markdown:
- **(a) No lock in 3.0.0; visible claims** (recommended). The orchestrator assigns parallel work, as today; a pushed task branch shows the task is taken; conflicts are reported. One small command.
- **(b) Exclusive locks now.** Needs renewal, hand-over and a way to stop a stalled agent that wakes up: a large task and a new way to fail, with no case yet that needs it.

blocks.title: What each release carries
3. What goes into 3.0.0?
blocks.markdown:
On 25 September you kept the docs line (EPC-016) and the autonomy line (EPC-018) in 3.0.0; on 26 September you moved them out to ship quickly. This gate removes that reason. The release candidate still accepts the presentation `diagram` block, which EPC-016 removes; publishing it makes the later removal a breaking change.

- **(a) Keep the split, retire the diagram input first** (recommended). Smallest release that never publishes something it plans to remove; one medium task.
- **(b) Fold the docs line into 3.0.0.** Waits for its open tasks (TSK-061 to TSK-063) and their reviews.
- **(c) Keep the split and publish the diagram block.** No work now; a breaking change in 3.1.

blocks.title: 4. When should the changelog move to one file per change?
blocks.markdown:
- **(a) In 3.1, through a new ADR** (recommended). 3.0.0 keeps the hardened single changelog; parallel lines keep conflicting on it until then.
- **(b) Now.** Ends the conflicts sooner, but reworks the release script while the release waits.
- **(c) Never.** The merge conflicts stay.

blocks.title: 5. How much live agent testing before release?
blocks.markdown:
- **(a) Six situations, three runs each, Claude and Codex: 36 sessions** (recommended). The strongest focused evidence of steady behaviour; failures are fixed and rerun. The most time; runs after the skills are rewritten.
- **(b) One run each: 12 sessions.** Quicker, but cannot tell steady behaviour from a lucky run; the release notes claim less.

blocks.title: 6. What happens to the EPC-015 line?
blocks.markdown:
The engineering-bar line (EPC-015, SPC-011, SPC-012) is merged nowhere, and no record says what happens to it.

- **Decide after the overlap list** (recommended): I bring what EPC-015 still holds and what this epic already covers, with the planning PR.
- Fold the overlap into EPC-020 and archive the rest.
- Land it separately after 3.0.0.
- Archive it.

blocks.title: Settled from evidence, unless you disagree
blocks.markdown:
- Every existing number is kept, including the legacy ones; only their format is fixed.
- Once a project tracks work, acceptance and journey checks can be set to block or warn, never off. This follows strict but adjustable, and it does remove an off switch.
- Small fixes can land without a task if the PR says why, except changes to contracts, policy, hooks or dependencies.
- The old `in_progress` status still reads but is no longer written.
